title: We run 100s of AI agents – here are the most common cyber attacks
content:
Security
The 7 most common attacks on website AI agents, and how to stop them
Across the hundreds of business websites where Javo runs AI agents, people try to hack them almost every day. Here are the 7 most common attack types, with real examples, what each one is after and how to protect an agent on WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Cloudflare or custom code.
Put an AI agent on a website and people will try to hack it. Javo runs AI agents on hundreds of business websites, and attack attempts arrive almost every day, often at least once per agent. Instead of asking about the business, the visitor tries to make the agent give up its instructions, its model or any API keys it can see.
The examples below are real messages sent to those agents in November 2026. The same tricks come back again and again, on every kind of site. Here is what each attack tries, what it is after and how to stop it.
The 7 most common attack types
Percentages are rounded, so they add up to slightly more than 100%. Attackers also send harmless messages such as “ping”, “say hi” or “what is 2+2”, sometimes many times in a row. These check that the agent responds and how fast, before or between attacks. They are not counted as attacks here. On Javo agents, every one of these messages, harmless or not, is logged, scored and visible to the team that owns the website.
What attackers are after
- The system prompt: the private instructions that say how the agent behaves, and sometimes contain prices, internal rules or customer details.
- Credentials: API keys and environment variables such as OPENAI_API_KEY. With a key, an attacker can run up your AI bill or reach your data.
- Cloud access: the metadata address 169.254.169.254 returns temporary credentials on many cloud servers. An agent that fetches any address a visitor gives it can hand those over.
- The model and provider: useful for picking attacks known to work on a given model.
- Your data flow: by putting an attack in the name field or the page address, attackers test whether data the agent reads, but that a person never typed into the chat, is trusted.
Why a refusal is not enough
A well-instructed agent will usually refuse politely and go back to its job: “I can’t share internal instructions, credentials, or environment variables. What’s your company’s website?” But a refusal is the last line of defence, not the first. A new wording can slip past it. Attacks fail for good when there is nothing to steal.
- No secrets in the prompt. If API keys stay on the server, the model never sees them and cannot repeat them, whatever trick is used.
- No tool to fetch addresses. An agent that cannot visit a URL a visitor gives it cannot be sent to a metadata address.
- Every field treated as untrusted. The visitor’s name, email and page address are data, not instructions.
- Attacks scored. A clear attack, such as a message starting with a fake “[SYSTEM]” tag, can get the sender blocked before they try many variations.
- Every conversation logged, so a person can see attacks and adjust.
This is how Javo’s website agents are built: keys stay on the server, the agent cannot fetch outside addresses, and a clear attack gets the sender blocked from every Javo chat for 30 days, with an alert to the team.
How to protect your own website agent
Javo agents follow the first six steps by default. If you build or buy another agent, check each one.
- Assume your system prompt will be read. Write nothing in it that you would not publish.
- Keep keys and credentials out of anything the model sees.
- Give the agent only the tools it needs. If it must fetch pages, allow a fixed list of domains and block private and metadata addresses.
- Treat form fields, page content, uploaded files and URLs as untrusted, not only the chat message.
- Do not let the agent act on claims of authority. A message that says it comes from your engineers is still a visitor message.
- Score messages and block repeat attackers automatically, with an alert to a person.
- Limit the number of messages per visitor, so scripted tests cannot run up your bill.
- Read the logs, and test your agent yourself with the prompts in the table above.
How to do it on your platform
Javo installs with one line of code on any of these platforms, and its keys stay on Javo’s servers, so nothing secret sits in your theme or page. If you run your own agent or a plugin, here is what to check.
Prompt injection is first on the OWASP list of risks for applications built on large language models, and system prompt leakage is on the same list. Any public chat will receive these messages. What matters is what the agent can reach when it does. Javo agents receive these messages every day on the websites they run on, and they are built so that a successful trick still finds nothing to take.

report.summary: Javo, which runs AI chat agents on hundreds of business sites, logs daily hacking attempts and outlines the seven most common attack types plus defences.
report.background: Businesses are rapidly deploying LLM-powered chat agents onto WordPress, Shopify, Webflow and custom sites, often wiring them to APIs, product data and cloud infrastructure. That makes the agent a new public-facing attack surface. Prompt injection sits at the top of the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, alongside system prompt leakage, and traditional web security tools were never designed to catch attacks written in natural language. Unlike a classic exploit, an injection needs no malformed request, just a persuasive sentence typed into a chat box. Attackers also probe with harmless messages like "ping" or "what is 2+2" to fingerprint the model and confirm the agent responds before launching real attempts. As agents gain tool access, the cost of a successful trick rises from leaked text to stolen API keys and cloud credentials.
key_points: Attackers overwhelmingly want three things: the hidden system prompt (which often contains pricing and internal rules), API keys such as OPENAI_API_KEY that can run up bills or expose data, and cloud credentials reachable via the metadata address 169.254.169.254. Any agent that fetches a visitor-supplied URL can be steered to that internal address.

Refusals are the last line of defence, not the first. A polite "I can't share internal instructions" can be defeated by rephrasing. The durable fix is architectural: keep secrets on the server so the model never sees them, and remove tools the agent does not genuinely need.

Untrusted input extends beyond the chat box. Names, email fields, page URLs and uploaded files are all data, not instructions. Attackers plant injections there to test whether content the agent reads, but no human typed into the chat, gets trusted by default.

Scoring and blocking beat endless prompt tweaking. A message opening with a fake "[SYSTEM]" tag is an obvious attack signal; Javo blocks such senders from every chat for 30 days and alerts the site team, which stops attackers cycling through variations.

Rate limits and logging matter as much as detection. Capping messages per visitor prevents scripted probing from inflating the AI bill, while full conversation logs let a human spot patterns and adjust defences over time.

Javo claims its agents follow the safe defaults by design: keys stay server-side, the agent cannot fetch external addresses, every field is treated as untrusted, and each conversation is logged and visible to the business owner.
report.impact: This is a practical reality check for the agentic AI boom. The industry has spent two years shipping agents with broad tool access and stuffing business logic into system prompts, often treating them as trusted insiders rather than public endpoints. Javo's data suggests attempted attacks are near-universal, not exceptional, so security has to be a default rather than a premium add-on. For developers, the lesson is that prompt-level guardrails are fragile and architectural isolation — secrets on the server, minimal tools, domain allowlists, blocked metadata addresses — is what actually holds. Expect procurement teams to start demanding these properties in AI vendor reviews, similar to how SOC 2 became table stakes. For regular users, the upside is safer chat widgets; the risk is that poorly built agents quietly leak internal pricing, customer data or credentials.
report.tools: To red-team your own agent, try promptfoo, NVIDIA's Garak vulnerability scanner, Microsoft PyRIT, and OWASP's LLM Top 10 checklist. For runtime defence: Lakera Guard, Rebuff, Guardrails AI and NeMo Guardrails for input/output filtering, plus Cloudflare AI Gateway for rate limiting and logging. On the infrastructure side enforce AWS IMDSv2 and egress allowlists to block metadata-address fetches. Javo itself is the vendor in the article, worth evaluating but not neutral.
